diagnostic_evidence.quote: Because of this, $p$ can have at most $q$ roots in the positive orthant, and thus it can have at most $q$ roots in $[\ell,u] \subset (0, \infty)$.
Letting $\ell$ and $u$ be the minimum and maximum singular values of $\mM$, our goal is now to find an odd polynomial $p$ so that $p(x)$ is as close to $1$ as possible on $[\ell,u]$.

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem imposes no condition on ℓ and u, but its supporting lemma and the Haar/equioscillation argument both assume ℓ, u > 0 (the Haar condition needs [ℓ,u] ⊂ (0,∞)), while the paper's setup lets ℓ = σ_min(M), which is 0 for rank-deficient M. At ℓ = 0 the argmin in the recursion is not unique (every odd p with 0 ≤ p ≤ 2 on [0,u] has error exactly 1), so p_t is ill-defined; for such p_t the theorem's defining relation u_{t+1} = max_{[ℓ_t,u_t]} p_t(x) contradicts its claimed evaluation u_{t+1} = 2−ℓ_{t+1} = 2 (e.g. p_t(x) = x/u_t gives max 1 ≠ 2). Relatedly, the matrix/scalar equivalence proof uses ‖polar(M)−p(M)‖ = max_{σ_i∈σ(M)}|1−p(σ_i)|, which fails for singular M under the rank-reduced definition of p(M) (the singular value 0 is dropped; e.g. M = 0 gives 0 ≠ |1−p(0)| = 1).

failure_location.quote: Let $d$ be odd and define $\ell_1 = \ell$ and $u_1 = u$. For $t = 1,\ldots,T$ define

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis 0 < ℓ ≤ u to Theorem 1 (and to the minimax problems and the equivalence in section:verification), noting that rank-deficient inputs are excluded or handled by a limiting/sup argument.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem 1 and the matrix/scalar equivalence are unreliable in the rank-deficient/degenerate regime ℓ = 0 that the setup admits; Theorem 2 inherits the ill-defined p* in that regime. All actual uses in the paper have ℓ > 0 (e.g. 10⁻³), so the loss is confined to the degenerate boundary.
issues.title: Theorem 1 lacks the hypothesis 0 < ℓ ≤ u; the degenerate case ℓ = 0 breaks the statement
issues.why_classification: Adding a standard local condition fixes the defect; the method, conclusions, rates, and advertised scope all survive, and only the degenerate ℓ = 0 boundary (never used in the paper) is excluded.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: for some $\widetilde{p}_1,\ldots,\widetilde{p}_{T-1} \in \mathbb{P}_{d}^{\odd}$. Let the image of $f$ on $[\ell,u]$ be $[a,b]$.

issues.failure_explanation: Competitor compositions of odd polynomials may have images on the non-positive side: e.g. f(x) = −x is a valid competitor with image [−u,−ℓ], so a/b = u/ℓ ≥ 1 > ℓ_T/u_T, i.e. the asserted inequality a/b ≤ ℓ_T/u_T is false for such f and the proof attempts to derive a contradiction from a true supposition. For a ≤ b ≤ 0 the rescaling factor c = 2/(a+b) is negative and the identity max|1−cf| = max{1−ca, cb−1} = (b−a)/(a+b) fails (with a = −u, b = −ℓ it yields the negative number −(u−ℓ)/(u+ℓ), whereas max|1−cf| = (u−ℓ)/(u+ℓ) > 0), so no contradiction is obtained; moreover the final chain's change of variables to [a/b,1] and the monotonicity step against [ℓ_T/u_T,1] are invalid when b ≤ 0 (the substitution produces [1, a/b] with a/b ≥ 1, and the relevant ratio is b/a, not a/b). The degenerate case a = b makes c undefined. No case distinction excluding or handling non-positive images appears anywhere in the proof. The theorem itself is true — a repaired induction exists (if 0 ∈ [a,b] the completion error is ≥ 1; on either side of 0, bounding the competitor's best approximation of a constant gives the correct one-sided ratio ≤ ℓ_T/u_T) — but as written the proof of the paper's central optimality result is incomplete and contains a false auxiliary claim.

failure_location.quote: We will prove that $\frac{a}{b} \leq \frac{\ell_T}{u_T}$  by contradiction.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Rewrite the induction to handle all possible images: keep the correct positive-image case (or rederive a/b ≤ ℓ_T/u_T from inductive optimality of best constant approximations); for images in (−∞,0] use the sign-flipped competitor and the ratio b/a; treat straddling images (error ≥ 1) and constant images (a = b) separately.
issues.overall_effect: The greedy-optimality claim (eq:optimal) and hence the paper's advertised worst-case optimality guarantee are unproven as written; Theorem 2's proof, which invokes Theorem 1, inherits the gap.
issues.title: Proof of Theorem 1 fails for competitors with non-positive images; the ratio sub-claim a/b ≤ ℓ_T/u_T is false
issues.why_classification: The theorem is true and the repair preserves the full optimality guarantee with the same induction architecture, but it requires a genuinely new case analysis and auxiliary comparison argument rather than a local edit, and it concerns the paper's central result.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Hence, for $d = 3$ the method converges quadratically and for $d = 5$ the method converges cubically.
Furthermore, the order of convergence of the degree $2q+1$ method is $q+1$ \cite{doi:10.1137/0708036}.

issues.failure_explanation: With d = 2q+1 the proof's exponent (d+1)^T = (2q+2)^T differs from the statement's (q+1)^T, yet the proof concludes 'as required'. The step invoking the Kenney–Laub bound with exponent (d+1)^T is false: the degree-d Padé/Newton–Schulz composition f has order q+1 per iteration (as the paper itself states in Related Work), giving exponent (q+1)^T. Concretely, for d = 3, T = 1, ℓ = 1/√2, the Newton–Schulz value f(ℓ) = (3/2)ℓ − (1/2)ℓ³ ≈ 0.884 satisfies |1−f(ℓ)| ≈ 0.116 > (1−ℓ²)^4 = 1/16, so the displayed inequality with (d+1)^T fails; for T = 3 the claimed bound 0.5^64 ≈ 5·10⁻²⁰ is far below the true greedy error (~10⁻⁶). Hence the proof chain establishes neither its own displayed bound nor, via this chain, the statement; the statement's (q+1)^T bound is the correct one and follows from the cited theorem with the right exponent.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace (d+1)^T by (q+1)^T in the two proof displays so that the invocation of the Padé-iteration convergence theorem matches its actual statement and the theorem's conclusion.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Theorem 2 is invalid as written (it endorses a false, stronger bound); the statement itself — order q+1, quadratic for d = 3, cubic for d = 5 — is correct and unaffected.
issues.title: Proof of Theorem 2 uses exponent (d+1)^T, contradicting the stated (q+1)^T bound and proving a false inequality
issues.why_classification: The statement, rate, and scope are unaffected; the repair is a forced local correction of the exponent in the proof (the statement, the order claims, and the cited theorem all force (q+1)^T, and the (d+1)^T version is demonstrably false).

diagnostic_evidence.quote: To this end, we make three small changes to the method.

issues.failure_explanation: The update ℓ_{t+1} = p_t(ℓ_t), u_{t+1} = 2−ℓ_{t+1} is justified (eq:newbounds, via Lemma computableerror) only for the exact minimizer of max|1−p| on [ℓ_t,u_t]. Algorithm 1 instead uses a polynomial optimized on the cushioned interval [max(ℓ_t,u_t/10),u_t] and then composed with x ↦ x/1.01, for which neither ℓ_{t+1} = min p_t nor u_{t+1} = 2−ℓ_{t+1} = max p_t is established. With the recommended parameters (ℓ₁ = 10⁻³, d = 5), the first cushioned polynomial maps ℓ₁ to a value of order 10⁻³–10⁻², so the recursion sets u₂ = 2−ℓ₂ ≈ 2, while the actual largest singular value after one step is p₁(u₁) = 1+E (well below 2); subsequent polynomials are then optimized for intervals ≈ [u_t/10, u_t] ≈ [0.2, 2] that no longer track the singular values, which drift outside [ℓ_t,u_t] and can grow without bound — the iteration as printed does not compute the intended method. The implementation that generated eq:coeffs and the experiments (Appendix G) contains an additional rescaling step (rescalar = 2/(p(ℓ_t)+p(u_t)), which makes u_{t+1} = p_t(u_t) up to the safety factor and maintains the invariant), but this step appears neither in Algorithm 1 nor among the 'three small changes' described in §4.4. Hence Algorithm 1 as printed is not the tested method and its implied interval invariant is unsupported.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Insert the rescaling step from the appendix code into Algorithm 1 (rescale each cushioned polynomial so that p_t(ℓ_t)+p_t(u_t) = 2 before applying the safety factor), mention it in §4.4's list of changes, and present the update rule as tracking the images of the interval endpoints (a valid overestimate up to the safety factor) rather than as a consequence of eq:newbounds; alternatively restrict the exact eq:newbounds recursion to the unmodified polynomials.
issues.overall_effect: Algorithm 1, the paper's central deliverable (advertised as a drop-in replacement and tied to the optimality story, e.g. the proof of Theorem 2 states it returns p*(M)), does not as printed maintain its singular-value bounds or reproduce the coefficients in eq:coeffs; a literal implementation misbehaves for the recommended parameters. The formal theorems concern the unmodified scheme and are unaffected.
issues.title: Algorithm 1's bound-update rule is invalid for its modified polynomials; the load-bearing rescaling step of the implementation is missing
issues.why_classification: The algorithm's operation fails as printed (the invariant breaks and the recommended instantiation does not compute the intended method), so more than a cosmetic edit is needed; however, the source itself contains the required construction (the rescaling step), no substantive claim must be abandoned, and the repair is contained within the algorithm block and its description.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: let $p^{\star}$ be the optimal approximation from $\mathbb{P}_{5}^{\odd}$ and let $p(x) = \frac{x/u}{8}\left(15-10(x/u)^2 + 3(x/u)^4\right)$.

Hence, when $\ell/u \geq 1-\epsilon_d^{1/3}$, where $\epsilon_{\text{double}} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-16}$ is the double precision machine epsilon, then $|p^{\star}(x) - p(x)| \leq 2 \epsilon_{\text{double}}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The step max_{[ℓ,u]}|1−p| ≤ (1−ℓ/u)³ is false: for u = 1, ℓ = 0.9 one has p(0.9) = (15·0.9 − 10·0.9³ + 3·0.9⁵)/8 = 0.99768, so max_{[ℓ,u]}|1−p| ≥ 0.00232 > (0.1)³ = 0.001. The correct consequence of the invoked Kenney–Laub theorem is max|1−p| ≤ (1−(ℓ/u)²)³/(1+p(ℓ/u)) ≈ (5/2)(1−ℓ/u)³ near ℓ/u = 1, so the claimed constant is too small by a factor ≈ 2.5. Consequently the derived conclusion |p*−p| ≤ 2ε_double for ℓ/u ≥ 1−ε_double^{1/3}, and the matching early-exit threshold in Algorithm 2, do not follow as stated (the correct statement carries a constant ≈ 5 instead of 2).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the constant: use max|1−p| ≤ (1−(ℓ/u)²)³/(1+p(ℓ/u)) (≈ (5/2)(1−ℓ/u)³), conclude |p*−p| ≤ 5ε_double, and adjust the early-exit threshold in Algorithm 2 accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The quantitative justification of Algorithm remezdeg5's early-exit branch (returning the scaled degree-5 Newton–Schulz polynomial when ℓ/u is close to 1) is wrong by a constant factor; the algorithm still returns an approximation to p* within a small multiple of machine epsilon, so the practical conclusion survives with adjusted constants.
issues.title: False constant in the Remez-appendix bound max|p*−p| ≤ 2(1−ℓ/u)³
issues.why_classification: A local constant-factor correction to an auxiliary estimate; the algorithm's behavior, the optimality results, and all substantive claims are preserved (the returned polynomial remains within machine-precision distance of the optimum up to a constant factor).
